passages.t: Bezalel and Oholiab, filled with the Spirit
passages.happening:
“See, I have called by name Bezalel son of Uri, the son of Hur, of the tribe of Judah. And I have filled him with the Spirit of God, with skill, ability, and knowledge in all kinds of craftsmanship” (verses 2-3). He is to work in gold, silver and bronze, to cut gemstones and to carve wood (verses 4-5).

“Moreover, I have selected Oholiab son of Ahisamach, of the tribe of Dan, as his assistant. I have also given skill to all the craftsmen, that they may fashion all that I have commanded you” (verse 6).

Then everything they are to make is listed: the tent, the ark and the mercy seat, the table, the lampstand, the two altars, the basin, the priests' garments, the oil and the incense (verses 7-11). “They are to make them according to all that I have commanded you” (verse 11).
passages.hearers:
The plans are finished. Since chapter 25 God has described the tent, its furniture, the priests' clothing, the oil and the incense. Now he names the people who will build it.

Bezalel is the first person in the Bible said to be filled with the Spirit of God. And what the Spirit gives him is skill with his hands: design, metalwork, stone cutting, wood carving. The Bible's picture of the Spirit's work is wider than many readers expect. It includes craft done well for God.

The word translated ‘skill’ is chokhmah, the ordinary Hebrew word for wisdom. In Hebrew a weaver or a metalworker can be wise. The three words of verse 3, skill, ability and knowledge, are the same three that Proverbs uses for how God made the world. The builders of the tent share, in a small way, the wisdom by which God built creation.

Think who these workers were. Not long before, they had been making bricks for Pharaoh. Egypt was known for its craftsmen, and some Israelites may have learned trades there. Much of the gold and silver came from what the Egyptians gave them as they left (12:35-36).

In the stories of Israel's neighbors, gods built houses for gods. In texts from Ugarit, on the coast of Syria, a craftsman god builds a palace for the storm god Baal. Exodus tells it another way. God designs his own dwelling, and ordinary people, filled with his Spirit, build it.

Bezalel is from Judah, the tribe that would lead the march. Oholiab is from Dan, a tribe usually listed among the lesser ones. The most honored tribe and one of the least work side by side. Whether Bezalel's grandfather is the Hur who held up Moses' hands (17:12) is possible, but the text does not say.
passages.later:
Moses repeats this to the people when the work begins, and adds that God gave both men “the ability to teach others” (Exodus 35:34).

Proverbs says, “The LORD founded the earth by wisdom and established the heavens by understanding. By His knowledge the watery depths were broken open” (Proverbs 3:19-20).

Paul writes of the Spirit's gifts in the church: “There are different gifts, but the same Spirit” (1 Corinthians 12:4), and “to each one the manifestation of the Spirit is given for the common good” (1 Corinthians 12:7). He also tells the church, “you yourselves are God’s temple” (1 Corinthians 3:16).
passages.asks: God called a craftsman by name and filled him with his Spirit for his work. Ask whether you think of your own work, with hands or mind, as something God's Spirit could fill. And ask who works beside you unnoticed, as Oholiab worked beside Bezalel, and how you could honor them.

passages.t: The Sabbath, a sign between God and Israel
passages.happening:
“Surely you must keep My Sabbaths, for this will be a sign between Me and you for the generations to come, so that you may know that I am the LORD who sanctifies you” (verse 13).

“Keep the Sabbath, for it is holy to you. Anyone who profanes it must surely be put to death” (verse 14). “For six days work may be done, but the seventh day is a Sabbath of complete rest, holy to the LORD” (verse 15).

“The Israelites must keep the Sabbath, celebrating it as a permanent covenant for the generations to come. It is a sign between Me and the Israelites forever; for in six days the LORD made the heavens and the earth, but on the seventh day He rested and was refreshed” (verses 16-17).
passages.hearers:
God has just told Israel how to build. Now he tells them when to stop building. Even the holy work of making God's house must rest on the seventh day.

This is the seventh and last of the speeches that began in chapter 25, and it is about the seventh day. Verse 17 makes the link with creation plain: in six days God made the heavens and the earth, and on the seventh he rested. The same Hebrew word for work runs through the chapter. It names Bezalel's craft, and it names the work that must stop. The work that honors God on six days honors him on the seventh by stopping.

The Sabbath is called a sign. A sign is something seen that points beyond itself, like the rainbow for Noah and circumcision for Abraham. Each marked a covenant. This sign is not an object. It is a day, made visible by what people stop doing.

It was Israel's plainest difference from its neighbors. Other peoples had festivals and lucky or unlucky days. A day of complete rest every seventh day, for everyone, servants and animals included, was Israel's own.

And the sign says something: ‘I am the LORD who sanctifies you’. Israel does not make itself holy by its work. God sets it apart, and the day of rest says so every week.

‘Was refreshed’ is a bold thing to say of God. The verb is related to the Hebrew word for breath, as if God caught his breath. The same verb was used in 23:12 of the servant's son and the foreigner. The rest God gives the least in Israel is pictured as his own.

Jewish tradition took the order of this chapter to heart. The Mishnah, compiled around AD 200, lists thirty-nine main kinds of work forbidden on the Sabbath, and the Talmud connects them with the kinds of work done to build the tabernacle. The Sabbath remains at the center of Jewish life today.
passages.later:
Genesis says, “by the seventh day God had finished the work He had been doing; so on that day He rested from all His work” (Genesis 2:2).

Ezekiel repeats this chapter almost word for word: “I also gave them My Sabbaths as a sign between us, so that they would know that I am the LORD who sanctifies them” (Ezekiel 20:12).

Jesus said, “The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath. Therefore, the Son of Man is Lord even of the Sabbath” (Mark 2:27-28).

Hebrews writes, “There remains, then, a Sabbath rest for the people of God” (Hebrews 4:9). Paul writes, “let no one judge you by what you eat or drink, or with regard to a feast, a New Moon, or a Sabbath” (Colossians 2:16).
passages.hard:
Why was breaking the Sabbath punished by death, and must Christians keep the Sabbath?

The penalty of verses 14 and 15 is severe, and it should be read soberly. Numbers records it carried out once, on a man found gathering wood (Numbers 15:32-36). Within this chapter's own reasoning, the Sabbath was the sign of the covenant. To work on it in open defiance was to renounce Israel's bond with God, in a nation whose king was God. That is nearer to treason than to a small offense. Later Jewish courts made a death sentence very hard to reach. The Mishnah records the view that a court which put someone to death even once in seven years was called destructive.

No Christian tradition applies this penalty, since the church is not a nation under Israel's law. It is not a pattern for anyone today. No one may use these verses to threaten or harm a person over how they keep a day.

On the second question Christians differ, and the note on Exodus 16 sets out the views more fully. Seventh-day Christians, among them Seventh Day Baptists and Seventh-day Adventists, hold that the command to rest on the seventh day still stands as given. The Reformed and Puritan tradition holds that the Sabbath continues, moved by Christ's resurrection to the first day of the week as the Lord's Day. Catholic, Lutheran and many other Christians hold that the seventh-day rest was a sign fulfilled in Christ, and they keep Sunday as the day of resurrection. And some, in dispensational and New Covenant traditions, hold that the covenant of Moses as a whole has been fulfilled in Christ, pointing to Colossians 2:16-17 and Romans 14:5.

These notes take no side. All of these agree that rest is God's good gift, and that it is not a way of earning his favor.
passages.asks: God told his people to stop even holy work one day in seven. Ask whether you can stop, or whether your worth depends on what you get done. And ask what it means that God is the one who sanctifies you, and that your work for him does not.

passages.t: Two tablets, written by the finger of God
passages.happening: “When the LORD had finished speaking with Moses on Mount Sinai, He gave him the two tablets of the Testimony, tablets of stone inscribed by the finger of God” (verse 18).
passages.hearers:
The forty days on the mountain end with a gift. Moses receives two stone tablets, called ‘the Testimony’, the tablets of the covenant. They are to be kept inside the ark (25:16).

‘The finger of God’ is a way of saying that these words came from God himself. Egypt's magicians had used the same phrase when they could not copy the plague of gnats (8:19). The power that judged Egypt now writes a covenant for Israel.

This verse is story, not law, and it turns the page. Moses stands on the mountain with the tablets in his hands. At the foot of the mountain the people have grown tired of waiting. God has been preparing a dwelling to his own design, to be built by craftsmen filled with his Spirit. The people are about to make a god to their own design, with their own gold.
passages.later:
Moses later tells Israel, “the LORD gave me the two stone tablets, inscribed by the finger of God” (Deuteronomy 9:10).

Jesus said, “if I drive out demons by the finger of God, then the kingdom of God has come upon you” (Luke 11:20).

Paul tells the Corinthians that they are a letter from Christ, “written not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God, not on tablets of stone but on tablets of human hearts” (2 Corinthians 3:3). Jeremiah had promised it: “I will put My law in their minds and inscribe it on their hearts” (Jeremiah 31:33).
passages.asks: God wrote his words in stone and put them in Moses' hands. Ask how you treat the words God has given you: as a weight, or as a gift. And ask what it would mean for those words to be written on your heart as well as on a page.
